title: A prayer that isn't hers
hook: Christ has no body now but yours is widely credited to Teresa but doesn't appear in her writings

segments.voice: Yesterday, mental prayer, which Teresa called a friendly conversation, often alone, with the one we know loves us. Did you find five minutes for that kind of conversation? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-six.

A bookmark in a parish gift shop. A poster in a hospital chapel. A slide at the end of a volunteer training. The words are lovely: Christ has no body now on earth but yours, no hands but yours, no feet but yours. And underneath, in small italic letters, a name. Teresa of Ávila. It's a prayer people print, frame and read aloud at funerals. There's only one problem with the name at the bottom. Today is about that problem, and about why someone who loves Teresa might care.
screen: `ON BOOKMARKS AND POSTERS.` → `CHRIST HAS NO BODY NOW BUT YOURS.` → `SIGNED: TERESA OF ÁVILA?`

segments.voice: The lines don't appear in Teresa's writings. Readers have looked through her Life, The Way of Perfection, The Interior Castle, her Foundations and her letters, and the prayer isn't there. Where it did come from isn't settled. So the name on the bookmark is a guess that hardened into a label. Does that make the prayer bad? No. Its idea runs straight back to Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." Catholics can treasure the thought and use it. The only thing wrong is the signature. Now compare a short verse that tradition does connect with her. It was found, the story goes, in her breviary, the book she prayed from, written in Spanish. It begins, let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you, and it ends, God alone is enough. Same saint, two very different paths to us: one with a trail you can follow, one without. Why care? Because a saint's real voice is worth hearing on its own terms. Teresa's own writing can be funny, sharp and demanding in ways a gift-shop quote is not. And because Scripture itself praises checking. The book of Acts describes the people of Berea, who heard Paul gladly but went home "daily searching the scriptures, whether these things were so." Paul tells another church: "prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Checking a source isn't cynicism. It's a way of taking the words, and the person, seriously.
screen: `NOT FOUND IN HER WRITINGS.` · `THE IDEA IS PAUL'S: THE BODY OF CHRIST.` · `A VERSE TRADITION TIES TO HER.` · `CHECKING IS A WAY OF HONORING.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one quotation's source. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a line you love, from a saint, a song, a poster, a parent. Ask yourself honestly: where do I know it from? Who actually said it? If you pray, you can thank God for the words, whoever first wrote them. If you don't, just hold the line and the question together. After the bell, if there's time, look it up and follow the trail. The bell holds the time.
A prayer that isn't hers. Christ has no body now but yours: a good thought, rooted in Paul, but not found in Teresa's writings. Today's word.
screen: `A PRAYER THAT ISN'T HERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: check the source. Today, before you share a quote, a post, or a story with a famous name on it, follow the trail back once. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics who study the saints read their words in critical editions of their writings, and Carmelite scholars note which popular sayings attributed to Teresa are not found there.

fork.setup: you're one of the Bereans. a traveling preacher named Paul has just told you something new. what do you do?
options: accept it on the spot because he sounds sure.
hear it gladly, then search the scriptures to see if it's so.
fork.reveal: Acts says they received the word eagerly and searched the scriptures daily, "whether these things were so." Acts praises them for it.

original.note: Spanish: God alone is enough. the closing line of the short verse tradition says was found in Teresa's breviary.

trapdoor: what you thought: Teresa wrote christ has no body now but yours.
what it means: the lines aren't in her writings. the idea is good, and Paul's, but the name on it is a guess.
what a scholar hears: a misattribution, with an origin not yet settled, set beside nada te turbe, a verse tradition links to her own breviary.

notes: The claim that 'Christ has no body now but yours' does not appear in Teresa's writings follows the outline's index line. The list of works searched is stated generally ('readers have looked'); confirm. The prayer's actual origin is left 'not settled' on purpose; a Keeper may know a documented source.
The Christ-has-no-body lines are paraphrased in the hook without quotation marks, since their wording and copyright status are uncertain.
'Nada te turbe' paraphrased in English ('let nothing disturb you... God alone is enough'); the breviary story is attributed to tradition. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Corinthians 12:27, Acts 17:11 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 to confirm.
Original: Spanish 'Sólo Dios basta' (older accented spelling; modern Spanish writes 'Solo'); confirm spelling and pronunciation.

Editor: 'written in her own Spanish' (implied her handwriting, which the tradition doesn't establish) changed to 'written in Spanish'; the comparative ranking of her writing over the gift-shop quote softened.
